newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac hopes power-sharing will serve France.
newsitem.headline: Chirac hopes power-sharing will serve France.

text.p: Conservative President Jacques Chirac met Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin's new cabinet for the first time on Thursday and said he hoped their power-sharing would be respectful and serve France's interests.

"France has just spoken, it has elected a new majority," Chirac told the "Pink-Green-Red" cabinet in his gilded Elysee Palace in his first public remarks since his centre-right coalition was routed in Sunday's National Assembly election.

"Here we are in a new period of 'cohabitation'. I do not doubt that it will take place in a dignified manner with mutual respect and a constant concern for France's interests," he told the 26-strong government, brimming with women and new faces.
Chirac will have to "cohabit", or share power, with Jospin's Socialist-led cabinet that includes Communist ministers for the first time since 1984 and a Green minister of the environment.

The Paris Bourse saluted a broadly pro-European government, in which Communists hostile to a European single currency were confined to the transport and sports ministries. The CAC-40 index was up 2.1 percent in early trading.

At the brief cabinet meeting, Chirac sat with a fixed smile at an oval table between Martine Aubry, the government's number two and minister of employment and social affairs, and Education Minister Claude Allegre.

Jospin said the talks went "well, very well" and he had spent much of the 30-minute meeting outlining his government's plans, which give top priority to combating record 12.8 percent unemployment. He said the atmosphere was both serious and relaxed.

Chirac gambled disastrously by calling the election 10 months ahead of schedule, hoping his centre-right allies would win re-election to give him five clear years of conservative rule until his own seven-year term expires in 2002.
Instead, he is the greatly diminished prisoner of a hostile majority and his own Gaullist party is in disarray.

Under France's two previous cohabitations, from 1986-88 and from 1993-95, late Socialist president Francois Mitterrand claimed pre-eminence in foreign affairs while leaving economics and other domestic issues to the government.
French media generally welcomed Jospin's cabinet, which ditched most of the "elephants" from Mitterrand's era.
"A government with a clean sweep," the conservative daily Le Figaro said with grudging admiration. "Good Luck!" the Communist daily L'Humanite said in a banner headline.
The apparently smooth start contrasted with the start of the first cohabitation in 1986 when Mitterrand vetoed the choices of Chirac, who was prime minister, for defence and foreign affairs.
"I felt as if I was surrounded by men of whom 60 percent hate me and 80 percent are fighting me. I was alone this morning, very alone," Mitterrand said of his first cabinet session with Chirac.
On the right, feuding intensified over the leadership of the Rally for the Republic party, founded by Chirac, with widening pressure for defeated prime minister Alain Juppe to stand down.
Former National Assembly speaker Philippe Seguin, a favourite of the right to succeed Juppe, formally announced he was putting forward his candidacy for the leadership.

Seguin, a leader of the narrowly-defeated "no" campaign when French voters approved the Maastricht treaty on European union in a 1992 referendum, said he would also stand as interim parliamentary floor leader of the party.
After the cabinet meeting, Jospin, 59, will make his first official trip abroad, going to the Swedish city of Malmo for a gathering of Socialist heads of government and parties.
He will address the conference on Friday and hold talks with Britain's new Labour Prime Minister Tony Blair, who swept to power in a landslide a month ago.
In a gesture of goodwill to Chirac, Jospin appointed two non-confrontational Socialists to the key foreign affairs and defence portfolios.
Hubert Vedrine, 49, a former Mitterrand chief-of-staff and diplomatic aide with long experience of managing "cohabitation", will be foreign minister. Alain Richard takes charge at defence.

New finance minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn will have to carry out promises of creating 700,000 youth jobs and cutting the working week to 35 hours from 39 with no loss in pay to attack the jobless total.
